name: Juvenile Localized Scleroderma (Linear Scleroderma)

criteria.description: Presence of linear bands of skin thickening and induration
No evidence of systemic sclerosis or systemic involvement
Skin biopsy showing dermal fibrosis with thickened collagen bundles
Presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) in some cases

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of linear skin thickening with absence of systemic sclerosis; biopsy supportive but not mandatory
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by histopathology; systemic involvement exclusion is essential

pathognomonic.notes: Typically unilateral, affecting limbs or face

pathognomonic.symptomName: Skin induration and thickening along linear bands
searchTerms: skin thickening and hardening along lines

pathognomonic.symptomName: En coup de sabre lesion on the forehead
pathognomonic.notes: Linear scleroderma affecting the frontoparietal scalp and forehead
searchTerms: forehead skin lesion resembling a sword strike
en coup de sabre forehead lesion
areas of lighter or darker skin within lesions
muscle wasting under affected skin areas
loss of muscle bulk beneath lesions
joint stiffness next to skin lesions
limited joint movement adjacent to lesions

common.symptomName: Facial hemiatrophy in linear facial lesions
searchTerms: one side of face with muscle and fat loss
facial asymmetry due to tissue wasting
hair loss over affected scalp areas

occasional.symptomName: Neurological symptoms such as headaches or seizures
occasional.notes: More common in en coup de sabre subtype
searchTerms: headaches and seizures as neurological symptoms
eye problems including inflammation inside the eye
eye involvement with redness and pain
presence of antinuclear antibodies in blood
localized swelling in early skin lesions

rare.symptomName: Severe neurological complications such as hemiparesis
searchTerms: severe neurological problems like weakness on one side
major neurological deficits including partial paralysis

rare.symptomName: Systemic symptoms such as fever or malaise

laboratory: Positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) in 30-50% of cases
Normal inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) in most cases
imaging: MRI may show soft tissue and muscle involvement underlying skin lesions
X-rays can reveal bone atrophy or deformities adjacent to lesions
genetic: No specific genetic mutation identified; possible polygenic predisposition
other: Skin biopsy demonstrating thickened collagen bundles and dermal fibrosis

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of systemic involvement including Raynaud phenomenon
Widespread skin involvement rather than linear localized plaques
Presence of epidermal nevi rather than sclerotic plaques

redFlags: Rapid progression of skin thickening with functional impairment
Neurological symptoms such as seizures or hemiparesis
Signs of systemic sclerosis or internal organ involvement
references: Mertens JS et al. Juvenile localized scleroderma: clinical and laboratory features in 750 children. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2017.
